case_study_insert.main_stem: Crestview Learning Group (CLG) is a private limited company in the education sector, running after-school numeracy centres and employing a workforce of 48. Founded in 2013 by Marcus Crest, it operates a hierarchical structure with autocratic leadership. CLG plans to invest $540,000 in six new numeracy learning centres, financed by a $300,000 bank loan and a $240,000 share issue. It has fixed costs of $270,000 a year, a variable cost of $15 a unit and a selling price of $60, and currently produces 12,000 units a year, each a funded course place. CLG faces two problems: tutor absenteeism has reached 8% and parent complaints about lesson quality at its centres are rising.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Extract — Q3 2025: CLG delivered 2,800 funded course places last quarter with a re-assessment pass rate of 86%, up from 79% a year ago. Parent complaints rose from 24 to 41 per month. Average lesson waitlist is 9 days. A survey of 450 parents found that 72% would pay $12 more per course for small-group tuition, and 61% choose providers by pass rates. Records show 12 of 48 tutors have not completed on-the-job training on the new numeracy software; accredited courses cost $650 per tutor.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Crestview Learning Group for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has cut the base interest rate from 5.0% to 4.4%, reducing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $13.50 to $14.31 per hour from April 2026, raising wage bills for tutoring staff. (3) School funding per pupil was reduced by 4.5% and education technology input costs rose 8.3%, while household spending on tutoring grew 3.1%.

questions.question_text: CLG plans to fund part of its $540,000 expansion with a $300,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for CLG of using a share issue rather than the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $240,000 share issue brings in equity that never has to be repaid and carries no compulsory interest, unlike the $300,000 bank loan. With contribution of $45 on each $60 course place, cash that would have serviced debt can instead cover the $270,000 fixed costs and the 8.3% rise in education technology input costs, protecting CLG's 12 places per tutor target without raising the price to parents.

Point 2: Share issue finance does not require collateral, so the six new learning centres cannot be repossessed if enrolment falls short, and it spreads financial risk among shareholders rather than leaving Marcus Crest's firm solely exposed. It also increases capital employed to $1,200,000, giving CLG a stronger equity base from which to borrow later, even though existing owners dilute their control.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to CLG's expansion financing and course-place economics.

questions.question_text: CLG is promoting its six new numeracy centres. Consider local radio advertising, printed school newsletters, or social media marketing. Which should CLG choose to attract parents? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local radio advertising: Radio is affordable and can reach parents during the school run within CLG's local catchment, and it suits a short message about new places. Its reach is confined to one area and listeners cannot easily compare CLG's 86% pass rate, so it will not build the volume needed to fill places created by the $540,000 expansion, and airtime is wasted on listeners without school-age children.

Printed school newsletters: Newsletters are cheap, land directly in the hands of parents and can carry detail on small-group tuition. They depend on schools agreeing to distribute them, reach only one school's families, have a short reading life and cannot demonstrate results, so on their own they are too narrow to recruit the 12,000 course places CLG targets.

Social media marketing: Targeted posts can reach parents in the exact catchments of the six new centres, show the 86% pass rate and the 72% of 450 surveyed parents willing to pay $12 more, and measure enquiries cheaply. The 61% who choose by pass rates can be given that evidence directly. Results take time to build and require careful, truthful content, but cost per enrolled parent is low and campaigns can be scaled centre by centre.

Recommendation: CLG should choose social media marketing. It targets parents precisely, supports the pass-rate message parents value and scales across six centres far better than radio or newsletters. Local radio is rejected as geographically limited and wasteful, and printed newsletters are rejected as too narrow and dependent on third parties; CLG can keep a small newsletter insert as a backup channel.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited identification of the promotional options with minimal reference to CLG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options with some application to CLG and partial judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options in CLG's context with a justified recommendation explaining why radio and newsletters are rejected.

questions.question_text: CLG's tutor absenteeism has reached 8% and parent complaints about lesson quality are rising. Explain two benefits for CLG of using financial motivators such as bonuses to improve tutor attendance.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Attendance bonuses give CLG's 48 tutors a direct financial reason to turn up reliably, attacking the 8% absenteeism rate. With each funded course place contributing $45, a tutor who avoids cancelled lessons protects revenue that covers $270,000 of fixed costs, and regular attendance keeps the 9-day waitlist from growing, which is one source of parent complaints.

Point 2: Performance-related bonuses reward the quality parents care about: the survey shows 61% choose providers by pass rates and 72% would pay $12 more for small-group tuition. Linking part of pay to the 86% re-assessment pass rate encourages tutors to prepare lessons well and to complete the numeracy software training that 12 of 48 still need, so CLG can justify the $540,000 centre expansion with better results.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation linked to CLG's absence, pass rates and expansion.

questions.question_text: CLG must train 12 tutors on the new numeracy software. Consider on-the-job training or accredited courses at $650 per tutor. Which should CLG choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching tutors inside the centres teaches CLG's own software and the small-group methods behind the 86% pass rate, costs no fees and keeps the 12 tutors teaching while they learn, protecting the 2,800 course places delivered last quarter. Senior tutors can mentor others and the training can be spread around the 9-day waitlist. The limits are that trainers are themselves tutors whose teaching time falls, bad habits may be copied, and there is no external certificate to reassure parents who choose by pass rates.

Accredited courses: At $650 per tutor, training 12 staff costs $7,800 (12 × $650), affordable against the $540,000 expansion. Courses bring current methods and a recognised qualification that strengthens CLG's credibility with the 61% of parents who choose by results. However, 12 of 48 tutors would be away from centres, worsening the 8% absenteeism and lengthening the 9-day waitlist, and generic course content may not match CLG's exact software, so follow-up coaching would still be required.

Decision: CLG should choose on-the-job training for most tutors and fund one accredited course for a lead tutor. On-the-job training is cheaper, directly relevant and avoids removing staff while absence is 8%; fully accredited training for all 12 is rejected because $7,800 and lost teaching time would hurt the waitlist and the $540,000 rollout for little added relevance.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited reference to CLG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods applied to CLG, including cost and disruption.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Full evaluation of both methods in CLG's context with a justified decision that rejects full external training and explains the cost and teaching-time trade-off.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CLG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $270,000 ÷ ($60 − $15) = $270,000 ÷ $45 = 6,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 6,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $60 − $15 = $45. Answer: contribution per unit is $45.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CLG's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 6,000-unit break-even output with 12,000 units actually produced: the margin of safety is 6,000 places, showing the centres can fill without loss and supporting the $540,000 investment.
2. Use the $45 contribution per $60 place to test pricing: the survey says 72% of parents would pay $12 more, so managers can weigh a price rise against enrolment rather than guessing.
3. Check that 6,000 break-even places generate enough contribution to meet the $300,000 bank loan commitment before opening all six centres.
4. Track unit cost of $37.50 per place ($270,000 ÷ 12,000 = $22.50 fixed plus $15 variable) to control the 8.3% technology cost inflation and to examine the fall in pass rate that drives the 41 monthly complaints.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 6,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $45 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 6,000 against 12,000 places; pricing using the $12 parent premium; servicing the $300,000 loan; and unit-cost benchmarking at $37.50.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CLG's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has CLG's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 45.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 50.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.5%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 17.5%

Detailed workings: Revenue increased from $1,200,000 to $1,400,000 while cost of sales rose only from $660,000 to $700,000, so gross profit went from $540,000 to $700,000. Gross profit as a share of revenue therefore improved from 45.0% to 50.0%. Operating profit grew from $150,000 to $210,000, lifting operating profit as a share of revenue from 12.5% to 15.0%. Capital employed rose from $1,000,000 to $1,200,000, giving a return on capital of 15.0% in 2024 and 17.5% in 2025.

Evaluation: Every measure improved, and the strongest gain is in the share of revenue retained after direct costs, suggesting good control of tutor delivery costs as the six centres came on stream. The operating result also improved, helped by spreading $270,000 of fixed costs over 12,000 places. However, interest payable rose from $25,000 to $35,000 as the $300,000 loan took effect, and capital employed grew faster than operating profit, so return on capital improved only modestly. Rising complaint numbers and 8% tutor absence could reverse these gains if lesson quality slips, and the extract shows no debt maturity detail.

Conclusion: CLG's financial performance has improved. Gross profit as a share of revenue rose from 45.0% to 50.0%, operating profit as a share of revenue from 12.5% to 15.0%, and return on capital from 15.0% to 17.5%. All three measures move upward together, so the improvement is well based, though higher interest cost and a small rise in return on capital mean management should watch the new centres' enrolment closely.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or directional changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with some contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs and capital employed and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CLG of offering small-group tuition at the new centres.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Small groups match parent demand. The survey found 72% of 450 parents would pay $12 more per course for small-group tuition and 61% choose providers by pass rates, so CLG can lift revenue above the $60 price and protect its $45 contribution while 8.3% technology costs rise. Smaller classes also support the 86% pass rate, helping justify the $540,000 expansion.

Disadvantage: Small groups need more tutors for the same 12,000 course places, raising the $15 variable cost per place or pushing fixed costs above $270,000. With tutor absenteeism at 8% and 12 of 48 untrained on the numeracy software, CLG may struggle to staff every group, lengthening the 9-day waitlist and adding to the 41 monthly complaints about lesson quality.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to CLG's survey, costs and staffing.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate cut to 4.4%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 8.3% rise in education technology costs will affect CLG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate cut (5.0% to 4.4%): This is a favourable change. If CLG's $300,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the rate falls by 0.6 percentage points, saving 0.6% × $300,000 = $1,800 a year. That is small compared with $270,000 of fixed costs, and if the loan is fixed-rate the saving is zero. Lower rates may also encourage parents to spend more on tutoring, but the direct cash benefit is limited and CLG cannot rely on rates staying low.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $14.31 an hour): CLG has a workforce of 48 and many tutor and support roles are hourly-paid, so this raises the wage bill and is unavoidable. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total cannot be honestly computed. The defensible test is productivity: 12,000 course places across 48 staff is 250 places per employee, so the rise is absorbable only if that output holds; otherwise the $37.50 unit cost rises and the $45 contribution per place shrinks.

Education technology cost inflation (8.3%): The $15 variable cost per place is not decomposed in the insert, so only a labelled illustrative upper bound is possible. If the whole $15 were exposed, 8.3% × $15 = $1.25 extra per place (to 2dp), and across 12,000 places that is about $14,940 a year (12,000 × $1.245), cutting contribution from $45 toward $43.75. CLG can offset part of this through the $12 premium that 72% of surveyed parents accept, and the pass-rate evidence they value.

Conclusion: The 8.3% rise in technology costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 12,000 course places and directly erodes the $45 contribution that funds the $540,000 expansion, and it is a cost increase that a rate cut cannot cancel. The minimum-wage rise is second but unquantifiable from the insert, while the interest-rate cut saves at most $1,800 and is the smallest effect of the three.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the three external changes with limited application to CLG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on CLG's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in CLG's context with a justified judgement that technology input costs have the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
